title: Introduction to AI-Assisted Development
subtitle: Build software faster with AI coding assistants without losing control: prompt for code, test and review everything it writes, catch hallucinations and security flaws, and ship a working prototype.
tools: AI coding assistant (Copilot, Cursor or similar)
outcomes: Write effective prompts for generating, refactoring and fixing code
Debug AI-generated code and catch hallucinated functions, packages and options
Finish the last 30% of a project test-first, with Git to roll back instead of patching
Review AI code for logic errors, style and security, with Ruff, Bandit and pip-audit
Prototype a web application with an AI assistant in planned, tested, documented steps
prerequisites: Basic Python (variables, functions, lists, dictionaries, running scripts), as in Python Programming with PyCharm, and a little Git. Install Python 3.10+, Git and a code editor, and pip install pytest ruff bandit pip-audit fastapi httpx uvicorn. You also need an AI coding assistant you're allowed to use, such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, JetBrains AI Assistant, Claude Code or a chat assistant; several have free plans, so check current terms.
description:
AI coding assistants can write a working first version of a feature in minutes, and then leave you stuck on the last 30%: the edge cases, the errors, the security holes and the bugs that appear when a fix for one problem breaks two others. This course teaches the habits that make AI-assisted development work. You'll learn how assistants behave and what they can see, then how to prompt for code with clear constraints, examples and small steps. You'll practise a feedback loop of prompt, run, test and commit; finish a half-working tool test-first; and roll back with Git instead of piling up patches, a habit the course calls 'roll, not fix'. You'll review generated code the way a senior developer would, finding hallucinated APIs, logic errors and security flaws with tests, Ruff and Bandit, and learn what licences and data policies mean for code an AI wrote.

The labs work with any AI coding assistant, such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, JetBrains AI Assistant, Claude Code or a chat assistant: each gives you a starting point and tests, so you can prove the result works whichever tool wrote it. The course ends with a capstone: a task manager web application, planned, built in slices, tested against an API contract and documented, including every hallucination you caught.

modules.title: Introduction to Vibe Coding
modules.summary: The shift from writing every line to guiding an AI: what vibe coding and AI-assisted development are, what assistants do well and badly, the feedback loop that keeps you in control, and what the assistant can actually see.

lessons.title: Vibe coding and AI-assisted development
objectives: Explain what vibe coding is and how disciplined AI-assisted development differs
Describe the main kinds of AI coding assistant
key_points: Vibe coding, a term coined in early 2025 by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, means building software by describing what you want to an AI and accepting its code with little reading: fast and fun for throwaway prototypes, risky for anything that matters.
AI-assisted development is the disciplined version: you guide the AI with clear goals, context and constraints, and you stay responsible for reading, testing and understanding everything you ship.

Assistants come in three broad forms: inline completion as you type, chat about your code, and agentic assistants that plan, edit several files and run commands or tests, such as Claude Code, Cursor's agent, GitHub Copilot's agent mode and JetBrains Junie.
Whatever the tool, your job shifts from typing every line to specifying, reviewing and verifying, so the skills that matter most are describing problems precisely and judging code critically.

lessons.title: AI as a collaborator: strengths and limits
objectives: Identify tasks AI assistants do well and the mistakes they typically make
Use assistants within your responsibilities and your organisation's rules
key_points: Assistants are strong at boilerplate, scaffolding, explaining unfamiliar code, writing tests and documentation, converting between formats or languages, and suggesting approaches you hadn't considered.

They make characteristic mistakes: functions, options or packages that don't exist, code for an older library version, plausible logic that fails on edge cases, insecure patterns from old examples, and confident explanations of wrong code.
They don't know your project's unwritten rules, users or constraints unless you tell them, and they can't judge whether a feature is the right one to build.
Treat the assistant as a fast, well-read collaborator whose work must be reviewed, not as an authority: you're accountable for every line you commit, including its security and its licence.
Follow your organisation's rules on which tools are allowed, and don't paste secrets, personal data or confidential code into a tool that isn't approved for it; check its data and training settings.

lessons.title: The feedback loop: prompt, generate, run, verify
objectives: Work in a tight loop of small prompts, runs, tests and commits
Give the assistant precise feedback from tests and errors
key_points: AI-assisted development works as a tight loop: describe one small change, let the assistant generate it, run the code and the tests, read the result, and feed back exactly what happened.
Small steps keep the loop fast and failures easy to locate; a prompt for a whole application at once produces more code than you can check.
Tests make the loop objective: a failing test, or the exact error message and traceback, is far better feedback than 'it doesn't work'.
Commit every known-good state with Git, so you can always get back to something that worked.
When the assistant keeps making things worse, return to the last good commit and start again with a better prompt instead of piling fix on fix; this course calls that habit 'roll, not fix'.

steps.do: Start a project folder under Git, with a virtual environment and pytest.
steps.code:
mkdir slug-lab && cd slug-lab
git init
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install pytest

steps.do: Commit the starting point before asking the assistant for anything.
steps.code:
git add .
git commit -m "Add slugify stub and tests"

steps.do: Ask the assistant for one small change, then run the tests.
steps.see: Either all tests pass, or failures whose messages you paste into your next prompt.

steps.do: When the tests pass, read the diff, then commit.
steps.code:
git diff
git commit -am "Implement slugify (AI-assisted, reviewed)"

steps.do: If a change makes things worse, throw it away and return to the last commit.
steps.see: Tracked files go back to the last commit; any new files the assistant created stay, and git status lists them.

lessons.title: Context windows: what the assistant can see
objectives: Explain what an AI assistant knows about your project and what it doesn't
Give an assistant the context a task needs, including standing project instructions
key_points: An assistant only knows what's in its context: your prompt, the conversation so far, the files or selection it was given or chose to read, and any project instructions; anything else, it guesses.
The context window is limited and measured in tokens, so in long sessions early details can be summarised away or dropped: start a fresh session for a new task and restate the key facts.
Give the context the task needs, such as the relevant files and signatures, exact error messages, library versions and conventions, and leave out what's irrelevant, which can distract it.

Project instruction files hold standing context for every session: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, .github/copilot-instructions.md for GitHub Copilot and rules in .cursor/rules for Cursor, and AGENTS.md is a shared convention that several tools read.
Never put secrets in prompts or instruction files, and check what an agentic assistant may read, run and change before you set it going.

lab.title: Your first AI feedback loop
lab.tool: AI coding assistant, Git and pytest
lab.goal: Set up a project under Git with your AI assistant, then use the prompt, run, test, commit loop to get an AI-written slugify() function through seven tests, feeding back failures until they all pass.
setup: Python 3.10 or newer, Git and pytest (pip install pytest)
Your AI coding assistant, set up in your editor or terminal
Download slugify.py and test_slugify.py into a new folder

steps.do: Initialise Git, make a virtual environment, install pytest, and commit the starter files.
steps.code:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Add slugify stub and tests"

steps.do: Run the tests to see the starting point.
Give your assistant the docstring and the tests (open both files, or paste them) and ask it to implement slugify() using only the standard library. Note your exact prompt.
Read the generated code before running it: which standard-library functions does it use, and do they exist? Then run the tests.
If anything fails, paste the failing test's output into your next prompt and ask for the smallest fix. Repeat until all seven pass, noting each prompt.
Review the diff and commit.
steps.code:
git diff
git commit -am "Implement slugify (AI-assisted, reviewed)"
git log --oneline

steps.do: Write a line that starts Loop: saying how many prompts it took and which feedback helped the assistant most.

checks.text: The starting point fails all seven tests.
The finished function passes all seven tests.
The work is committed in two steps.
Each prompt is recorded, and a Loop: line reflects on the feedback that helped.

files.content:
"""Turn titles into URL slugs. Ask your AI assistant to implement slugify() from this docstring and the tests."""


def slugify(text: str, max_length: int = 60) -> str:
    """Return a URL slug for text.

    - Lower-case ASCII letters, digits and single hyphens only: "Hello, World!" -> "hello-world"
    - Accented letters lose their accents: "Crème brûlée" -> "creme-brulee"
    - No hyphens at the start or end; an input with no letters or digits gives ""
    - If the slug is longer than max_length, cut it at the last hyphen that fits ("one-two-three", 9 -> "one-two");
      a single word longer than max_length is simply cut to max_length
    """
    raise NotImplementedError

hints: unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', text) splits accented letters into a base letter and an accent, which encoding to ASCII with errors='ignore' then drops.
If test_cut_at_a_hyphen fails, show the assistant that test and the docstring's rule about cutting at the last hyphen that fits.
Run pytest from the folder that holds both files, so the test can import slugify.

modules.title: Prompting Techniques for Developers
modules.summary: Prompts that produce code you can use: clear goals, context, interfaces and constraints; zero-, one- and few-shot examples; big tasks broken into small steps; and iterating from what comes back.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a good code prompt
objectives: Write a code prompt with a goal, context, interface, constraints and expected format
Use acceptance criteria and plans to keep generated code on target
key_points: A good code prompt states the goal, the context (language and version, framework, files involved), the interface (function signature, inputs, outputs, examples), the constraints and the format of the answer you want.
Constraints prevent unwelcome surprises: no new dependencies, follow the existing style, raise ValueError on bad input, keep the public interface unchanged, add type hints.
Say what form you want back, such as only the function, a unified diff, tests first, or a short plan before any code, so the reply is easy to review.
Acceptance criteria, ideally as tests, tell both the assistant and you when the job is done.
For a bigger task, ask the assistant to ask clarifying questions or propose a plan first: agreeing a plan is cheaper than reviewing the wrong code.

lessons.title: Zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompts for code
objectives: Choose between zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompts for a coding task
Use examples and tests to pin down behaviour
key_points: A zero-shot prompt describes the task with no examples, which works for common, well-specified tasks such as 'write a function that removes duplicate items from a list, keeping their order'.
A one-shot prompt shows one example to follow, such as an existing endpoint or test in your project's style: 'add a /tasks endpoint like this /notes one'.
A few-shot prompt gives several input and output examples, which pins down behaviour that's hard to describe, such as what a parser should accept and reject; examples written as tests do double duty.
Choose examples that cover the edge cases, not just the easy ones, and watch for the assistant copying details of an example that should differ.

lessons.title: Break big tasks into small prompts
objectives: Decompose a feature into steps that can be generated and tested separately
Plan with the assistant before implementing
key_points: Large requests produce large, tangled answers: break a feature into steps, such as the data model, the core functions, the API and then the interface, with tests at each step.
Give each prompt one concern and a clear interface to the others, so each piece can be generated, reviewed and tested on its own.
Ask the assistant for a numbered plan, review and edit it, then implement it one step at a time; agentic tools often have a planning mode for exactly this.
Review each step's diff before moving on: a problem is cheapest to fix in the step that caused it.

lessons.title: Iterate on prompts from the output
objectives: Evaluate generated code against the requirements before trusting it
Give specific feedback, and know when to start again
key_points: Read the first output critically: does it meet every requirement, handle the edge cases, use real APIs and match your style? Run it before you trust it.
Give specific feedback: what's wrong, what you expected, and the exact error or failing test; 'test_invalid fails because "10" is accepted' works far better than 'still wrong'.
Add the constraint you forgot rather than arguing with the output, and ask for alternatives with their trade-offs when you aren't sure which approach is best.
If you're going round in circles, start a fresh session with a better first prompt that includes what you've learned, and save prompts that worked for reuse.

lab.title: Prompt for a parser three ways
lab.tool: AI coding assistant, Git and pytest
lab.goal: Get an AI assistant to write parse_duration() three ways, with a zero-shot prompt, a few-shot prompt and a plan-then-implement prompt, compare the results against 14 tests, and keep the best version lint-clean.
setup: Python 3.10 or newer with pip install pytest ruff
Download durations.py and test_durations.py into a new folder under Git

steps.do: Commit the starter files, then run the tests.

Zero-shot: in a fresh session, ask for parse_duration(text) -> int that turns durations such as '1h30m' into seconds, without showing the tests. Save the code as a branch or a copy, and run the tests.

Few-shot: in a fresh session, give the same request plus examples of valid and invalid inputs (the test cases are good ones), and the constraints: standard library only, type hints, ValueError for invalid input. Run the tests.
Decomposed: in a fresh session, ask first for a plan (the rules for valid input, then the parsing steps), correct the plan if needed, then ask for the code. Run the tests.
Keep the version that passes all 14 tests (iterating with the failing test output if none does), then lint it and commit.
steps.code:
python -m pytest -q
ruff check durations.py
git commit -am "Add parse_duration"

steps.do: Write a short prompt log with lines starting Zero-shot:, Few-shot: and Decomposed:, each giving the prompt and the number of tests it passed first time.

checks.text: The final parse_duration() passes all 14 tests.
The final version is lint-clean.
The prompt log compares the three techniques by first-time test results.
The few-shot prompt states the constraints and includes invalid examples such as '30m1h'.

lab.submit: Paste your prompt log, the final durations.py, and the pytest and ruff output.

files.content:
import pytest

from durations import parse_duration


@pytest.mark.parametrize("text, seconds", [
    ("90s", 90),
    ("15m", 900),
    ("2h", 7200),
    ("1h30m", 5400),
    ("1h 30m 15s", 5415),
    ("1H30M", 5400),
    (" 45m ", 2700),
])
def test_valid(text, seconds):
    assert parse_duration(text) == seconds


@pytest.mark.parametrize("text", ["", "abc", "10", "5x", "-5m", "30m1h", "1h1h"])
def test_invalid(text):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        parse_duration(text)

hints: Zero-shot answers often accept '10' as ten seconds, or '30m1h': the tests say both are invalid, which only examples or explicit rules can tell the assistant.
A fresh session for each technique keeps the earlier prompts from leaking into the comparison.
If ruff reports a finding you don't understand, ask the assistant to explain the rule, then check the rule's page in Ruff's documentation.

modules.title: Overcoming the 70% Problem
modules.summary: Push past the quick first version to software that works: why the last 30% is hard, targeted prompts for bugs and edge cases, test-driven development with an assistant, and keeping people in charge of the design, with Git to roll back.

lessons.title: Why the last 30% is hard
objectives: Explain the 70% problem in AI-assisted development
Recognise the work that remains after a quick first version
key_points: The 70% problem, a pattern described by software engineer Addy Osmani, is that AI gets you a working-looking first version fast, while the last stretch, such as edge cases, error handling, integration, performance, security and maintainability, takes most of the effort.
The first version usually handles the happy path the prompt described; real data, real users and real systems bring the cases nobody mentioned.
Developers without the background to see what's missing can get stuck in loops where each AI fix breaks something else.
The way through is engineering discipline: specify the edge cases, test them, change one thing at a time and keep the design under human control.

lessons.title: Targeted prompts for bugs and edge cases
objectives: Turn a bug into a precise, reproducible prompt
Find edge cases deliberately instead of waiting for users to hit them
key_points: Reproduce first: a failing test or a minimal input that shows the bug turns a vague complaint into a precise target.
Give the assistant the failing test or input, the full error and traceback, the relevant code and the expected behaviour, and ask it to explain the cause before it proposes a fix.
Ask for the smallest change that fixes this bug and keeps the other tests passing, and fix one bug at a time.
List edge cases deliberately: empty and missing values, boundaries, unusual formats, unexpected types, very large inputs and non-English text, and ask the assistant for others you might have missed.

lessons.title: Test-driven development with an assistant
objectives: Apply the red-green-refactor cycle with an AI assistant
Spot an assistant gaming the tests
key_points: Test-driven development (TDD) runs in short cycles: write a failing test (red), write just enough code to pass it (green), then tidy the code with the tests still passing (refactor).
With an assistant, you own the tests as the specification: write or carefully review them, then ask the assistant to make them pass without changing them.
Watch for an assistant gaming the tests: special-casing the test inputs, weakening assertions, catching every exception, or deleting a test that fails.
Run the whole suite after every change, because a fix for one case can break another; a coverage tool such as coverage.py shows code that no test exercises.

lessons.title: Human oversight and 'roll, not fix'
objectives: Keep architectural decisions with people, and record them
Roll back a bad generation with Git instead of patching it
key_points: Keep architectural decisions with people: the data model, the boundaries between components, the dependencies, security and error handling shape everything that follows and are costly to change later.
Use the assistant to propose options with their trade-offs, then decide, and record the decision and its reasons in a short architecture decision record (ADR).
Commit small, working steps, and try risky changes on a branch (git switch -c experiment), so a failed experiment is easy to drop.

Roll, not fix: when a generation goes wrong, restore the last good commit (git restore, or git reset --hard to discard every uncommitted change) and prompt again with what you learned, rather than asking for fix after fix.

steps.do: See what the assistant changed before deciding what to keep.
Throw away the changes to one file, or to every tracked file.
steps.see: The files are back as they were at your last commit.

steps.do: List the new files the assistant created, then delete them if you don't want them.
steps.code:
git clean -n    # only lists
git clean -f    # deletes
steps.see: git clean -n changes nothing; -f deletes the untracked files it listed.

steps.do: Try a risky change on its own branch, and drop the branch if it fails.
steps.code:
git switch -c try-new-parser
# ...prompt, test...
git switch main      # or master
git branch -D try-new-parser

modules.title: Reviewing and Debugging AI Code
modules.summary: Develop a critical eye for generated code: review it like a pull request, catch hallucinated APIs and packages, enforce style with linters, find security flaws with static analysis, and handle licences.

lessons.title: Review AI code like a colleague's pull request
objectives: Review AI-generated code systematically before committing it
Use a checklist to make reviews consistent
key_points: Never accept AI-generated code you haven't read: review it as you would a colleague's pull request, diff by diff, before it's committed.
Check that it does what was asked and nothing more, handles errors and edge cases, has clear names and no duplication, comes with tests, and adds no dependency you didn't expect.
Ask the assistant to explain anything you don't understand, but check the explanation against the code, the documentation and a test.
Use a checklist so reviews are consistent, and keep changes small enough to review properly: a 2,000-line diff can't be reviewed well.

lessons.title: Hallucinations in code: APIs, packages and versions
objectives: Recognise hallucinated functions, options and packages
Verify unfamiliar code against documentation and by running it
key_points: Code hallucinations include functions or options that don't exist, such as isoformat(timespec="minute") where Python expects "minutes", methods borrowed from another library, and features of a different version.
Check unfamiliar calls against the official documentation for the version you use, and run the code: many hallucinations fail at once, but some only on a particular input.

Assistants sometimes suggest packages that don't exist, and attackers can publish malicious packages under such names (sometimes called slopsquatting), so confirm a package is the real, maintained one before installing it.
Pin dependency versions in a requirements or lock file, and tell the assistant which versions you use so its code matches them.

lessons.title: Style, consistency and static analysis
objectives: Use formatters, linters and type checkers to keep generated code consistent
Run security and dependency scanners on a project
key_points: Style guides such as PEP 8 keep code readable, and formatters such as Ruff's formatter or Black apply layout automatically, so reviews can focus on substance.
Linters such as Ruff find likely bugs and bad patterns, such as unused imports and undefined names, and type checkers such as mypy or Pyright catch type errors before the code runs.
Security linters such as Bandit for Python, and multi-language tools such as Semgrep and CodeQL, flag risky patterns like SQL built from strings, eval(), shell=True and weak hashes.
Dependency scanners such as pip-audit check installed packages against databases of known vulnerabilities, and secret scanners find keys committed by mistake.
Run these tools in pre-commit hooks and in CI, and put your style rules in the assistant's instruction file so generated code starts closer to your standards.

walkthrough.title: Lint, scan and audit a project

steps.do: Install the three tools into the project's environment.
Lint and check formatting.
steps.see: Findings with rule codes, such as F401 for an unused import, or All checks passed!

steps.do: Scan for security problems, skipping the virtual environment.
steps.see: Issues with IDs such as B608 (SQL built from strings), each with a severity and a confidence, or No issues identified.

steps.do: Check the installed packages for known vulnerabilities (this needs an internet connection).
steps.see: Vulnerable packages with the versions that fix them, or a message that none were found.

lessons.title: Security flaws to look for, and licences
objectives: Find and fix common security flaws in generated code
Explain the licensing and policy questions AI-generated code raises
key_points: Prevent injection: build SQL with parameterised queries, never f-strings, and run commands without shell=True, passing their arguments as a list.
Never run untrusted input through eval() or exec(), or load it with pickle; parse it with a strict parser such as int() or json.loads() instead.
Keep secrets out of code and repositories: read them from environment variables or a secrets manager, and treat any key that was ever committed as exposed, replacing it.

Hash passwords with a slow, salted algorithm such as scrypt (in Python's hashlib), bcrypt or Argon2, never MD5 or SHA-1; watch too for disabled TLS checks, path traversal and over-permissive CORS. The OWASP Top 10 lists the most common web risks.

Generated code can closely match licensed code: some tools can block or flag suggestions that match public code, copyleft licences such as the GPL carry obligations, and the copyright status of AI output is unsettled in many places, so follow your organisation's policy.

"""A small notes store that an AI assistant generated in one go. It runs, but don't ship it: review it first.

Usage: python notes_app.py
"""
import hashlib
import os
import pickle
import sqlite3
import subprocess
from datetime import datetime

SECRET_KEY = "change-me-123"


def connect(path="notes.db"):
    db = sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, owner TEXT, title TEXT, body TEXT, created TEXT)")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, password_hash TEXT)")
    return db


def add_user(db, name, password):
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", (name, hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest()))


def add_note(db, owner, title, body):
    created = datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="minute")
    db.execute("INSERT INTO notes (owner, title, body, created) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", (owner, title, body, created))


def search(db, owner, term):
    query = f"SELECT title FROM notes WHERE owner = '{owner}' AND title LIKE '%{term}%' ORDER BY id"
    return [row[0] for row in db.execute(query)]


def page(db, owner, number, size=10):
    """Notes for one page of results, counting pages from 0."""
    titles = [row[0] for row in db.execute("SELECT title FROM notes WHERE owner = ? ORDER BY id", (owner,))]
    return titles[number * size: number * size + size - 1]


def word_count(expression):
    """Lets users type sums such as '120 + 30' to total word counts."""
    return eval(expression)


def export(db, owner, folder):
    data = pickle.dumps(search(db, owner, ""))
    subprocess.run(f"mkdir -p {folder}", shell=True)
    with open(os.path.join(folder, f"{owner}.pickle"), "wb") as f:
        f.write(data)


def import_notes(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return pickle.loads(f.read())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    db = connect(":memory:")
    add_user(db, "amina", "s3cret-pass")
    for i in range(12):
        add_note(db, "amina", f"Note {i}", "...")
    print(search(db, "amina", "Note 1"))

import json
import sqlite3

import pytest

import notes_app


@pytest.fixture
def db():
    db = notes_app.connect(":memory:")
    for i in range(12):
        notes_app.add_note(db, "amina", f"Note {i}", "...")
    notes_app.add_note(db, "bilal", "Bilal's private plan", "...")
    return db


def test_add_note_records_the_time(db):
    created = db.execute("SELECT created FROM notes LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0]
    assert len(created) == 16  # YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM


def test_search_finds_titles(db):
    assert notes_app.search(db, "amina", "Note 1") == ["Note 1", "Note 10", "Note 11"]


def test_search_cannot_be_tricked_into_showing_other_owners_notes(db):
    assert notes_app.search(db, "amina", "%' OR owner = 'bilal' --") == []


def test_pages_hold_ten_notes(db):
    assert len(notes_app.page(db, "amina", 0)) == 10
    assert notes_app.page(db, "amina", 1) == ["Note 10", "Note 11"]


def test_passwords_are_not_stored_as_md5(db):
    notes_app.add_user(db, "amina", "s3cret-pass")
    stored = db.execute("SELECT password_hash FROM users").fetchone()[0]
    assert stored != notes_app.hashlib.md5(b"s3cret-pass").hexdigest()
    assert notes_app.check_password(db, "amina", "s3cret-pass")
    assert not notes_app.check_password(db, "amina", "wrong")


def test_word_count_adds_numbers_without_eval():
    assert notes_app.word_count("120 + 30 + 5") == 155
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        notes_app.word_count("__import__('os').getcwd()")


def test_export_and_import_use_json(db, tmp_path):
    path = notes_app.export(db, "amina", tmp_path / "out")
    assert json.loads(path.read_text())[:2] == ["Note 0", "Note 1"]
    assert notes_app.import_notes(path)[:2] == ["Note 0", "Note 1"]

modules.title: Prototyping with AI Assistants
modules.summary: Put it all together to build a prototype quickly and safely: an architectural plan first, an AI-made scaffold, features in tested vertical slices, and a record of what the AI contributed.

lessons.title: Start with an architectural vision
objectives: Write a one-page plan before generating code
Use the plan and acceptance tests to steer the assistant
key_points: Before generating code, write a one-page plan: the users and their problem, the features in this version and what's out of scope, the data model, the components and the technology choices.
Give the plan to the assistant as context, for example in ARCHITECTURE.md or the project's instruction file, so every prompt builds towards the same design.
Ask the assistant to critique the plan and list risks and open questions before any code exists: changing a plan takes minutes, changing code takes hours.
Define acceptance tests for the main features early, such as the API contract, so 'done' is measurable.

lessons.title: Scaffold the project with AI
objectives: Scaffold a project with an assistant and check what it produced
Keep a scaffold minimal and runnable
key_points: Use the assistant to scaffold the structure: folders, a dependency file, an application skeleton, a test set-up, a README and a .gitignore.
Check that every dependency it adds is real, current and needed, pin the versions, and make sure the skeleton runs and its first test passes before adding features.
Commit the scaffold as your first known-good state.
Keep scaffolding minimal: generated boilerplate you don't understand is code you'll still have to maintain.

lessons.title: Build in vertical slices, testing each step
objectives: Build features as end-to-end slices with tests and commits
Refactor safely as the prototype grows
key_points: Build one feature at a time from end to end, such as its data, API, interface and test, so there's always a working version to demonstrate.
For each slice: prompt for the smallest change, run the tests, try it by hand, review the diff and commit, then start the next slice.
Refactor when duplication or confusion appears, with the tests as a safety net, and update the plan when you learn something that changes it.
When a slice goes wrong, roll back rather than letting problems pile up across several features.

lessons.title: Document the AI's contributions
objectives: Keep an AI log of prompts, outputs and manual changes
Disclose AI assistance in commits and documentation
key_points: Keep an AI log as you work: the tool, what you asked for, what it produced, what you changed by hand and why, the hallucinations you caught and the tests you ran afterwards.
The log makes reviews easier, shows what you learned, supports honest disclosure, and helps trace where code came from if questions about quality or licensing come up later.
Record AI assistance in commit messages or trailers where your team asks for it; some tools add a Co-authored-by trailer automatically.
Finish with a README that says how to install, run and test the project, and what it can't do yet.

lab.title: Prototype an API in vertical slices
lab.tool: AI coding assistant, FastAPI and pytest
lab.goal: Plan, scaffold and build a habit tracker API with an AI assistant, one slice at a time against eight acceptance tests, committing each slice and logging what the AI contributed.
setup: Python 3.10 or newer with pip install fastapi httpx uvicorn pytest (if a warning asks for httpx2, install that too)
Download test_api.py, ARCHITECTURE.md and AI_LOG.md into a new folder under Git

steps.do: Read test_api.py and finish ARCHITECTURE.md: the slices, the data model and your decisions. Commit it.
Ask the assistant to critique the plan and list risks, giving it ARCHITECTURE.md and the tests. Update the plan if it finds something real.
Ask for a minimal scaffold: app.py with an empty FastAPI app and a reset() function, plus requirements.txt. Run it and open the interactive docs.
Slice 1: prompt for creating and listing habits only, run the tests (slice 2 and 3 tests still fail), review the diff, commit, and add a row to AI_LOG.md.
Slice 2: check-ins, counted once per day, and 404s for unknown habits. Test, review, commit and log.
Slice 3: current and longest streaks, and validation of dates. Test, review, commit and log.
Run the whole suite and look at the history.
steps.see: 8 passed, and a commit per slice.

steps.do: Write a line that starts Slices: saying what building in slices caught that one big prompt would have hidden.

checks.text: All eight acceptance tests pass.
The plan is written before the code, with the slices and decisions.
Each slice is committed separately and logged in AI_LOG.md with what was changed by hand.
A Slices: line reflects on what building in slices caught.

lab.submit: Paste ARCHITECTURE.md, app.py, AI_LOG.md, the output of pytest -q and git log --oneline, and your Slices: line.

# Habit tracker: architecture (fill this in before you prompt)

## Users and the problem
Who uses it, and what they need to do.

## Features in this version (and what is out of scope)
1. Create and list habits
2. Check in on a day (once per day)
3. Current and longest streak

## Data model
Habit: id (int), name (non-empty text), check_ins (set of dates)

## Components
- API: FastAPI app in app.py, data held in memory (a database later)
- Tests: test_api.py, run with pytest

## Decisions (and why)
- Dates as ISO strings (YYYY-MM-DD) in the API, validated as dates

hints: The tests import app and reset from app.py: reset() must empty the in-memory store so each test starts clean.
FastAPI returns 422 automatically when the request body fails validation, such as a day that isn't a date.
-k slice_1 runs only the tests whose names contain slice_1.

study_plan.focus: How AI-assisted development works; set up your assistant, Git and pytest, and finish the feedback-loop lab.
Prompting techniques for developers: constraints, examples, decomposition and iteration; finish the parser lab.
Tackle the 70% problem test-first, then review, debug and secure AI-generated code; finish both labs.
Prototype in slices, then build and present the task manager capstone, and review with the mock exam and flashcards.

project.title: AI-assisted task manager prototype
project.brief: Design and build a prototype task manager web application with an AI coding assistant, and document how you did it. Start from ARCHITECTURE.md: the users, the features in this version, the data model, the components and your decisions. The backend is a FastAPI app that must pass the acceptance tests in test_tasks_api.py (creating tasks with validation, listing and filtering by status, updating, deleting and 404s), plus at least three tests of your own. The frontend, served by the backend or built with a framework you know, must let a user add, edit, complete, filter and delete tasks. Write the prompts that generate the frontend and the backend yourself, building in vertical slices with a commit per slice. Keep AI_LOG.md as you go: each prompt, what the assistant produced, what you changed by hand, every hallucination or bug you caught and how you refined the prompt, and at least one roll-back. Before you finish, review the code, run Ruff and Bandit and fix their findings, and check every dependency is real and pinned in requirements.txt. Finally, present the prototype in a short written walkthrough: what it does, how to run it, and what you would do next.
deliverables: ARCHITECTURE.md, written before the code and updated as decisions changed
The backend, passing all eight acceptance tests and at least three tests of your own
A frontend that adds, edits, completes, filters and deletes tasks through the API
AI_LOG.md with at least eight entries, including the hallucinations caught and a roll-back
A git history with a commit per slice, and clean Ruff and Bandit output
README.md with setup, run and test instructions, and a short walkthrough of the prototype

rubric.name: Plan and architecture
rubric.description: A clear plan written first, with scope, data model, components and reasoned decisions that the code follows.

rubric.name: Working backend and tests
rubric.description: All acceptance tests pass, the learner's own tests cover meaningful edge cases, and errors are handled properly.

rubric.name: Frontend
rubric.description: The interface supports every task operation, shows errors usefully and works with the API as documented.

rubric.name: Process and AI log
rubric.description: Slices are committed one at a time; the log records prompts, manual changes, hallucinations and a roll-back honestly, with the prompt refinements they led to.

rubric.name: Review and security
rubric.description: Ruff and Bandit are clean, dependencies are real and pinned, and no secrets are in the code.

rubric.name: README and walkthrough
rubric.description: Someone else can install, run and test the app from the README, and the walkthrough explains what it does and what comes next.

project.submit: Paste ARCHITECTURE.md, your backend code and tests, the main frontend files, AI_LOG.md, the output of pytest, Ruff and Bandit, your git log --oneline, and your README with the walkthrough.

"""Acceptance tests for the task manager API. Your backend must pass them. Run: pytest -q test_tasks_api.py

They expect a FastAPI app object called app in app.py, and a reset() function that empties the data store.
"""
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from app import app, reset

client = TestClient(app)


def setup_function():
    reset()


def new(title="Write report", **extra):
    return client.post("/api/tasks", json={"title": title, **extra})


def test_create_task_with_defaults():
    r = new()
    assert r.status_code == 201
    body = r.json()
    assert body["title"] == "Write report" and body["status"] == "todo" and body["due"] is None
    assert isinstance(body["id"], int)


def test_title_is_required():
    assert client.post("/api/tasks", json={"title": "  "}).status_code == 422
    assert client.post("/api/tasks", json={}).status_code == 422


def test_due_date_must_be_a_date():
    assert new(due="2026-11-30").json()["due"] == "2026-11-30"
    assert new(due="next Friday").status_code == 422


def test_list_and_filter_by_status():
    new("A")
    b = new("B").json()
    client.patch(f"/api/tasks/{b['id']}", json={"status": "done"})
    assert [t["title"] for t in client.get("/api/tasks").json()] == ["A", "B"]
    assert [t["title"] for t in client.get("/api/tasks", params={"status": "done"}).json()] == ["B"]


def test_update_title_and_status():
    t = new().json()
    r = client.patch(f"/api/tasks/{t['id']}", json={"title": "Write final report", "status": "doing"})
    assert r.status_code == 200
    assert r.json()["title"] == "Write final report" and r.json()["status"] == "doing"


def test_status_must_be_known():
    t = new().json()
    assert client.patch(f"/api/tasks/{t['id']}", json={"status": "finished"}).status_code == 422


def test_delete_task():
    t = new().json()
    assert client.delete(f"/api/tasks/{t['id']}").status_code == 204
    assert client.get(f"/api/tasks/{t['id']}").status_code == 404


def test_unknown_task_is_404():
    assert client.get("/api/tasks/999").status_code == 404
    assert client.patch("/api/tasks/999", json={"status": "done"}).status_code == 404
    assert client.delete("/api/tasks/999").status_code == 404
